newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels on the move again, fear over refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels on the move again, fear over refugees.

text.p: Zaire's rebel war flared again with defence ministry officials saying on Sunday rebels were advancing in the east and may have overrun a town from which some 25,000 Hutu refugees have apparently fled.
After a week of tentative efforts to negotiate an end to the four-month civil war in eastern Zaire, the focus swung sharply back to the battlefield with a new rebel drive on Kalima town.

"I was told that the situation at Kalima was worrying and informed that there were rebels advancing on that road," one senior official told Reuters in the capital. "There were only a few Zairean soldiers there so if it has fallen it would not suprise me, but I cannot confirm it."

The officials were commenting on the war for the first time since U.N. officials reported the disappearance of the Kalima refugees. The refugees likely abandoned their camp and fled into the forest because of fear of escalating fighting.
The Belgian who leads mercenaries fighting for the Zaire government said on Sunday rebels currently held the upper hand.
Christian Tavernier also accused Uganda of supporting the rebels, fighting to overthrow Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko's 31 year-rule, taking their war deep into the vast nation.
"There are well-organised armed units coming from Uganda who carry out an operation, attack a position, and then retreat," Tavernier told Belgian radio RTBF.
"That means...the balance of strength is currently against us," he said on the telephone from eastern Zaire.
He added: "The Zairean army is in a tangle, like the rest of the country, with almost no logistics."
Defence sources said a significant number of the mercenaries had left Zaire. They gave no reason but Tavernier's surprise interview hinted at disillusion.
The government has consistently maintained that the estimated 300 Serb, French, Belgian and other armed foreign nationals in the region were operating merely as instructors.
Sources close to the mercenaries said that around 30 of them left Zaire two weeks ago, some of them suffering from dysentery.

The mercenaries were concentrated in January in the northeastern area of the war zone but proved unable to withstand the firepower of the rebels, whom Zaire said were backed up regular Ugandan army soldiers. Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi deny Kinshasa's charges that their troops had joined the rebels.
With the war going so badly, the Zaire government has become increasingly touch about news reports and on Sunday expelled a Swiss journalist it accused of telling lies.
Jean-Philippe Ceppi, who was sent to Zaire by French daily Liberation, was held in the Shaba Province capital Lubumbashi on Thursday, and escorted on a plane to Kinshasa the next day.
"They said I had not respected the proper protocol, and acccused me of telling lies," Ceppi told Reuters just before leaving Kinshasa for Johannesburg on Sunday.
Senior aid officials in Kinshasa in contact with the region said missionaries confirmed Kalima had been taken by the rebels.
The U.N. refugee agency on Sunday asked Zaire's government to allow it to carry out an aerial search for the refugees.
The frontlines had been relatively quiet since South Africa and regional states launched initiatives last week for talks.
"Our reinforcements are at (nearby) Kindu where there are even some warplanes, so we can expect a response shortly," the senior defence official said.

President Mobutu Sese Seko, currently at his villa in the south of France, named General Mosala Modjandongo, commander of the Lower Zaire region, to take charge of Zaire's land forces, state radio reported on Saturday.
